challenges.name: query-keys-invalidation-quiz
challenges.title: Which queries does an invalidation reach?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the enrollment incident: an invalidation that never matched, and what invalidateQueries really refetches.

questions.explanation: True. invalidateQueries compares the filter key with each cached key element by element, from the start: "enrollment" and "enrollments" are different strings, so no query is marked stale, nothing refetches, and no error is reported. The POST succeeded, which is why the button looked fine and only the other tab was wrong. A key factory (enrollmentKeys.byUser(userId)) used by both useQuery and the invalidation turns a typo into a compile error or makes it impossible. The misconception is that an invalidation that matches nothing fails loudly; it silently does nothing.

questions.question:
After saving a course in the admin page:

await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["courses"] });

TanStack Query Devtools just before the call:
["courses","list",{"category":"react"}]   1 observer   (on screen)
["courses","list",{"category":"node"}]    0 observers  (inactive)
["courses","detail","c_214"]               0 observers  (inactive)

Statement: "With the default options, this call immediately sends three GET requests, one for each cached query under [\"courses\"]."
questions.explanation: False. In TanStack Query v5, invalidateQueries marks every matching query as stale, but by default (refetchType: "active") it refetches only the queries that are currently rendered, here the react list: one GET. The two inactive queries stay in the cache marked stale and refetch when a component uses them again. So a broad invalidation is cheaper than it looks on a quiet page and expensive on a dashboard with many mounted queries, which is how the over-eager fix reached 40 requests per click. Check it in the Network panel and in Devtools, where invalidated queries turn stale. The misconception is that invalidate means refetch everything now.

challenges.name: query-keys-invalidation
challenges.title: Query key factory and invalidation after a mutation
challenges.description: After a learner enrolled, the catalog's My courses tab kept showing Enroll until a full reload; the first fix invalidated every query after every mutation and refetched 40 queries per click. Write the key factories and keysToInvalidate. (1) normalizeFilters(filters) turns URL filters into a canonical object: keep category only if it is react, node, sql, python or devops; level only if beginner, intermediate or advanced; page only if it is an integer greater than 1 (page 1 is the default); search trimmed and lower-cased, only if not empty; sort only if it is newest or rating (popular is the default; any other value is dropped). Every other property is dropped. Add the kept properties in alphabetical order (category, level, page, search, sort), so equal filters give identical keys. (2) courseKeys.all = ["courses"], courseKeys.lists() = ["courses", "list"], courseKeys.list(filters) = ["courses", "list", normalizeFilters(filters)], courseKeys.details() = ["courses", "detail"], courseKeys.detail(id) = ["courses", "detail", id], enrollmentKeys.all = ["enrollments"], enrollmentKeys.byUser(userId) = ["enrollments", userId]. (3) keysToInvalidate(cachedKeys, mutation) returns the cached keys, in cache order, that start with one of the mutation's target keys, compared element by element (an element matches when it is deep-equal; a longer cached key below a target matches too, a string that merely begins with the same characters does not). Targets: enroll and unenroll -> courseKeys.detail(courseId) and enrollmentKeys.byUser(userId) (lists are not invalidated: catalog cards may show the enrolled count up to a minute late); edit -> courseKeys.detail(courseId), courseKeys.lists() and enrollmentKeys.all (My courses shows titles); publish -> courseKeys.lists(); any other mutation type -> nothing. The runner prints courseKeys.list(f) for each f of { "filters": [...] }, or keysToInvalidate(cache, m) for each m of { "cache": [...], "mutations": [...] }, as JSON.
hints: Two separate questions: when are two filter objects "the same request" for the server, and when does a mutation make a cached answer wrong? The first is answered by normalizeFilters, the second by a small table from mutation type to target keys.

Look at how the keys are built: courseKeys.list starts with courseKeys.lists(), which starts with courseKeys.all, so a target such as ["courses", "list"] is a prefix of every list key. Then look at how you compare a target with a cached key: position by position, with the target no longer than the key. Joining a key into one string such as "courses/detail/c_1" and calling startsWith treats "c_1" as a prefix of "c_10".

A similar factory for a different feature: leaderboardKeys.all = ["leaderboard"], leaderboardKeys.period(p) = ["leaderboard", p]. With the cache [["leaderboard","weekly"], ["leaderboard","weekly","page",2], ["leaderboard","weekly-2025"], ["users","u_7"]], invalidating the target ["leaderboard","weekly"] returns the first two keys only: the third has a different second element, and the fourth a different first one.

tests.name: Equal filters give equal keys: property order, defaults and spaces do not matter
The incident: enroll refreshes the course and the user's enrollments, not every query
Edit and publish reach every list; unenroll only the course and the enrollments
Element prefix, not string prefix: c_1 must not reach c_10, c_1-intro or user u_10
URL filters: unknown params, invalid values, page 0, a string page, upper-case search
An unknown mutation type and a mutation that matches nothing invalidate nothing
Large cache: 155 keys, enroll touches 2 of them, edit reaches 60 lists, 3 users and 1 course
